name: Buenos Aires
tagline: Tango, Malbec and midnight dinners in the Paris of the south
description:
Buenos Aires feels like a European capital that drifted south and learned to stay up late. Wide boulevards lined with Belle Époque mansions and jacaranda trees lead to leafy plazas, grand old cafés and a bookshop in seemingly every other doorway, while tango still drifts out of dance halls where couples glide across the floor until three in the morning.

Every barrio has its own swagger. Cobbled San Telmo is all antique markets and street-corner tango, Recoleta hides a city of marble tombs where Eva Perón rests, and La Boca's corrugated-iron houses blaze in primary colors around the Caminito. Palermo, the biggest neighborhood, is the place for design shops, lush parks, cocktail bars and restaurants that don't fill up until well after 10 p.m.

Life here revolves around the table. Parrillas slow-grill beef over wood embers, pizzerias pile on mozzarella with abandon, and every café serves buttery medialunas alongside a cortado. Friends pass around mate gourds in the park and Malbec flows freely. Days start late and nights end at dawn, so pace yourself, embrace the siesta and let the city's passion for football, theater and spirited debate sweep you along.

safety.notes: Generally safe for a big city, but pickpockets and phone snatchers target tourists in San Telmo, the Microcentro and on the Subte. In La Boca, stick to the Caminito strip and the stadium area, and leave before dusk.

tipping: Leave about 10% in cash at restaurants, since card tips often can't be added, and don't be surprised by a small 'cubierto' cover charge for bread and table service.
gettingAround: The Subte metro and a vast colectivo bus network run on the rechargeable SUBE card, and contactless bank cards also work at many gates. Ecobici bikes and protected lanes make cycling easy, and taxis or ride apps are affordable for late nights.
tips: Pay larger bills with a foreign credit card, which usually gets a fair exchange rate, and keep some pesos for tips, taxis and markets since ATMs charge steep fees and have low limits.
Dinner starts around 9:30 p.m., so book for 8 p.m. only if you enjoy an empty dining room, and have a merienda of coffee and pastries around 5 p.m. to tide you over.
Buy a SUBE transit card at a kiosk or Subte station on day one; buses don't take cash.
At the Recoleta Cemetery, grab a map at the entrance, as the lanes are a maze; Evita lies in the Duarte family vault, usually marked by fresh flowers.
Teatro Colón's upper-tier standing and gallery tickets for opera and ballet can cost less than the guided tour, so check the season calendar early.
Tap water is safe to drink, and cafés will happily bring a small glass of soda water with your coffee.
etiquette: Porteños greet with a single kiss on the right cheek, including men greeting male friends.
If you're offered mate, drink the whole gourd and hand it back without touching the straw; saying 'gracias' means you don't want any more.
Steer clear of casual jokes about the Falklands, which locals call Las Malvinas; it remains a deeply felt subject.
Locals dress smartly even for casual dinners, so leave the athletic wear for the park.

neighborhoods.name: Palermo
neighborhoods.blurb: The city's largest barrio splits into Soho's boutiques and cobbled plazas, Hollywood's restaurants and cocktail bars, and vast parks with lakes and rose gardens.

neighborhoods.name: San Telmo
neighborhoods.blurb: Cobblestones, colonial facades, antique shops and a famous Sunday street fair, with tango dancers performing on Plaza Dorrego at dusk.

neighborhoods.name: Recoleta
neighborhoods.blurb: Elegant and Parisian in feel, with grand mansions, luxury boutiques, top museums and the extraordinary cemetery of marble mausoleums.

neighborhoods.name: Villa Crespo
neighborhoods.blurb: A down-to-earth neighborhood of leather outlets, old bodegones and a fast-growing scene of natural-wine bars and chef-driven bistros.

neighborhoods.name: Puerto Madero
neighborhoods.blurb: Restored red-brick dockside warehouses and glassy towers along the canals, with riverside promenades, steakhouses and the wild Costanera Sur reserve next door.

dishes.name: Asado
dishes.description: A slow-cooked feast of beef cuts, sausages and sweetbreads grilled over wood embers, served with chimichurri and endless conversation.

dishes.name: Empanadas
dishes.description: Baked or fried pastry turnovers filled with hand-cut beef, ham and cheese or creamy sweetcorn, eaten by hand as a snack or starter.

dishes.name: Choripán
dishes.description: A split chorizo sausage grilled until crackling and tucked into crusty bread with chimichurri, sold from carts at parks and football stadiums.

dishes.name: Alfajores
dishes.description: Soft sandwich cookies glued together with dulce de leche and often dipped in chocolate, found in every kiosk and bakery.

dishes.name: Mate
dishes.description: A bitter herbal infusion sipped through a metal straw from a shared gourd, passed hand to hand among friends as a ritual of hospitality.

events.name: Buenos Aires International Book Fair
events.description: One of the biggest book fairs in the Spanish-speaking world fills the La Rural exhibition grounds with author talks, readings and publishers for three weeks.

events.name: Tango Buenos Aires Festival y Mundial
events.description: Two weeks of free concerts, classes and milongas culminate in the world tango championship, where couples from across the globe compete.

events.name: La Noche de los Museos
events.description: For one night, hundreds of museums, cultural centers and galleries open free until the early hours, with extra buses and huge crowds.

events.name: Marcha del Orgullo
events.description: Buenos Aires Pride fills the Avenida de Mayo with floats, music and hundreds of thousands of marchers heading to Plaza de Mayo.

attractions.name: La Boca
attractions.description: The old port barrio, where immigrants once daubed their tin-clad houses with leftover ship paint, is now a riot of color along the Caminito, with tango dancers, painters and souvenir stalls. Football fans can tour La Bombonera, home of Boca Juniors, a few blocks away.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive by taxi or ride app, stay on the main Caminito strip and around the stadium, and head out before dusk.

attractions.name: Recoleta Cemetery
attractions.description: A labyrinth of marble mausoleums, weeping angels and Art Nouveau chapels where presidents, poets and generals rest, and where fresh flowers always appear at Eva Perón's family vault. Wandering its lanes, with cats sunning themselves on the tombs, is oddly serene.
attractions.bookingTip: Pick up a map at the gate or join a guided walk, since the lanes form a maze; come early to beat tour groups.

attractions.name: Teatro Colón
attractions.description: Regularly ranked among the world's finest opera houses for its acoustics, the Colón dazzles with a horseshoe auditorium of red velvet and gold leaf beneath a painted dome. Guided tours reveal the gilded foyers, but nothing beats hearing an opera or ballet from the upper tiers.
attractions.bookingTip: Book guided tours online a few days ahead, and check the season calendar for affordable upper-tier performance tickets.

attractions.name: Plaza de Mayo
attractions.description: Argentina's political heart is framed by the pink Casa Rosada, the colonial Cabildo and the cathedral where the late Pope Francis once served as archbishop. On Thursday afternoons, the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo still march in white headscarves for those who disappeared under the dictatorship.
attractions.bookingTip: The Casa Rosada runs free guided tours on weekends; reserve online in advance and bring your passport.

attractions.name: San Telmo
attractions.description: The city's oldest barrio is a tangle of cobbled lanes, crumbling colonial houses and antique dealers, anchored by an iron-and-glass market hall. On Sundays, the Defensa street fair stretches for more than a kilometer with vintage soda siphons, leather goods, buskers and tango on Plaza Dorrego.
attractions.hours: Sunday fair about 10:00–17:00; market hall daily
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive on Sunday before noon to browse ahead of the crowds, and stay for the evening open-air milonga on Plaza Dorrego.

attractions.name: MALBA
attractions.description: A sleek limestone-and-glass museum devoted to Latin American art, where Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Tarsila do Amaral and Antonio Berni share the walls. Its excellent café and art-house cinema make it an easy half-day in Palermo.
attractions.bookingTip: Wednesdays bring reduced admission and later hours; buy tickets online to skip the weekend line.

attractions.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
attractions.description: A 1919 theater turned bookshop, where shelves fill the former boxes and balconies and a café occupies the old stage beneath a painted ceiling and crimson curtains. It's one of the most beautiful bookstores on Earth, and browsing costs nothing.
attractions.bookingTip: Visit on a weekday morning for crowd-free photos, and order a coffee on the stage for the best view of the auditorium.

attractions.name: Bosques de Palermo
attractions.description: A sprawling green lung of lakes, eucalyptus groves and jogging paths centered on a rose garden with some 18,000 bushes. On weekends, porteños paddle-boat, rollerblade and share mate on the lawns, and the nearby Japanese Garden makes a calm, koi-filled detour.
attractions.bookingTip: Grab an Ecobici or a paddle boat on a weekday afternoon, and bring mate and pastries for a picnic like the locals.

attractions.name: Costanera Sur Ecological Reserve
attractions.description: Built on rubble dumped into the river decades ago and reclaimed by nature, this wild reserve of lagoons, pampas grass and willow thickets shelters hundreds of bird species. Its trails lead to the muddy-brown Río de la Plata, with the towers of Puerto Madero at your back.
attractions.bookingTip: Cycle the main loop to cover more ground, then refuel with a choripán from the grill carts outside the gates.

attractions.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
attractions.wiki: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Buenos Aires)
attractions.description: Argentina's national fine arts museum pairs Goya, Rembrandt, Van Gogh and Rodin with a superb collection of Argentine painting, from gaucho scenes to Berni's bold collages. Entry is free, making it an ideal rainy-afternoon stop after the Recoleta Cemetery.
attractions.bookingTip: Head upstairs first for the Argentine collection, which most visitors rush past on their way out.

hotels.name: Mansión Ombú Recoleta
hotels.description: A French-style Belle Époque mansion with a sweeping marble staircase, a glass-roofed winter garden and suites furnished with antiques and supple Argentine leather. Afternoon tea and a heated rooftop pool look out over Recoleta's mansard roofs.

hotels.name: Casa Glicina Palermo
hotels.description: A 1920s townhouse behind a wisteria-draped facade, with nine rooms around a garden patio, a small plunge pool and an honesty bar stocked with Mendoza wines. Palermo's parks, boutiques and bars are all a pleasant walk away.

hotels.name: Hostel Mate Amargo
hotels.description: A rambling colonial house with soaring ceilings, bunk dorms and a rooftop terrace where the weekly asado draws travelers from every continent. Free tango and Spanish lessons run in the patio.

hotels.name: Hotel Pampa Concreto
hotels.description: Raw concrete, pale leather and gaucho-inspired textiles define this minimalist hotel a short walk from MALBA. Rooms have rain showers and floor-to-ceiling windows, and the rooftop bar mixes inventive Fernet cocktails.

hotels.name: Hotel Cúpula de Mayo
hotels.description: A restored early-1900s hotel on the grand avenue leading from Plaza de Mayo, with wrought-iron cage elevators, stained-glass skylights and a domed corner suite. The ground-floor café still serves medialunas at marble tables, just as it did a century ago.

hotels.name: Balcones de Barrio Norte
hotels.description: Spacious French-style apartments with parquet floors, full kitchens and balconies over busy, tree-lined Avenida Santa Fe. They suit longer stays, with a supermarket downstairs and the Subte on the corner.

restaurants.name: El Carrito de Don Lolo
restaurants.description: A smoke-billowing grill cart by the reserve gates, serving juicy chorizo in crusty bread with a help-yourself bar of chimichurri and salsa criolla. Grab one after a bike ride and eat at the plastic tables along the river promenade.
restaurants.signatureDish: Choripán with chimichurri and salsa criolla

restaurants.name: Pizzería Fugazzeta Mía
restaurants.description: A bustling Avenida Corrientes counter where locals eat standing up, working through thick slices oozing mozzarella with a wedge of fainá chickpea flatbread on top. Theater crowds pour in the moment the curtain falls.
restaurants.signatureDish: Fugazzeta (onion and mozzarella stuffed pizza) with fainá

restaurants.name: Confitería El Almendro
restaurants.description: Bow-tied waiters, polished wood and mirrored walls set the scene for café con leche and buttery medialunas at this old-world confitería. Linger over the newspaper as long as you like; nobody will rush you.
restaurants.signatureDish: Café con leche with three medialunas

restaurants.name: Tierra de Humo
restaurants.description: A dozen courses cooked entirely over wood, ember and smoke trace Argentina from Patagonian lamb and king crab to northwestern llama and native Andean potatoes. The wine pairing explores high-altitude Salta and cool-climate Patagonian vineyards.
restaurants.signatureDish: Patagonian lamb slow-cooked over embers with smoked eggplant

restaurants.name: Parrilla La Tranquera Roja
restaurants.description: A classic grill house where the parrillero tends a wood-fired grill longer than the bar, turning out bife de chorizo, crispy sweetbreads and molten provoleta. Order a bottle of Malbec and ask for your steak 'jugoso' if you like it pink.
restaurants.signatureDish: Bife de chorizo with provoleta and chimichurri

restaurants.name: Cantina El Conventillo Azul
restaurants.description: Checked tablecloths, football pennants and waiters bellowing orders set the mood in this old immigrant cantina a few steps from the Caminito. Portions are enormous, so share a milanesa napolitana and a plate of homemade sorrentinos.

restaurants.name: Sofra Ereván
restaurants.description: A warm family dining room celebrating Palermo's Armenian community with lamb keppe, stuffed vine leaves, crisp lahmajun flatbreads and syrup-soaked baklava. Weekend nights bring live oud music.

restaurants.name: Cepa Nocturna
restaurants.description: A candlelit cellar bar with more than 300 Argentine labels, from Patagonian Pinot Noir to Salta Torrontés, poured by sommeliers keen to steer you beyond Malbec. Pair your flight with cured meats, Patagonian cheeses and warm empanadas.
restaurants.signatureDish: Tucumán-style beef empanadas with a Malbec flight

experiences.name: Milonga Night Tango Class
experiences.description: Learn the embrace and basic walk in a friendly beginners' class, then follow your teacher into a traditional milonga to watch, and maybe join, porteños dancing into the small hours. Nobody expects perfection, just respect for the dance floor's unwritten codes.

experiences.name: Bares Notables Café & Bodegón Crawl
experiences.description: Hop between century-old cafés and a smoky bodegón on and around Avenida de Mayo, tasting empanadas, provoleta, vermouth with soda and alfajores. Your historian guide unpacks immigration, politics and poetry at every marble table.

experiences.name: Tigre Delta Kayak & Island Asado
experiences.description: Swap the city for the maze of rivers and stilt houses in the Paraná Delta, paddling quiet channels with a local guide. The day ends with a riverside asado on an island reachable only by boat.

experiences.name: Palermo Street Art by Bike
experiences.description: Pedal the protected bike lanes of Palermo, Colegiales and Villa Crespo with an artist guide who introduces the murals, stencils and stories behind them. The ride finishes at a craft brewery with a pint on the house.
